justification_text:
The point estimates across all horizons were driven by underlying assumptions about stability in the system being modeled. Specifically, I assumed that while some level of variability or noise would occur over different time horizons, the central tendency of the outcome—represented here as the point estimate—would remain constant at 166.5. This reflects a base-case scenario where there are no strong signals or anticipated events suggesting a directional shift in the mean outcome over time. Essentially, I relied on historical data or prior observations indicating that the system tends to remain anchored near this value unless disrupted by new and significant information.

The confidence interval widths were dictated by the expected accumulation of uncertainty over time. In shorter time frames, such as one day, outcomes tend to stay closer to the central estimate due to limited time for deviations or external shocks to exert influence. As the time horizon extends to one week or one month, uncertainty grows because more variables come into play, including compounding effects, potential shifts in trends, or the materialization of risks. This is why the 90% confidence interval starts out narrow for the one-day horizon (166.5 ± 3.33) but expands substantially over one month (166.5 ± 12.65). The broadening reflects the fact that unpredictability typically increases as the forecast range extends.

However, specific risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. Unexpected shocks—such as geopolitical events, major policy announcements, or unforeseen system failures—would not have been captured in these intervals if they were not probabilistically built into the model. Additionally, structural changes in the system that invalidate the historical baseline assumptions used for the forecast could also push outcomes beyond the 90% confidence intervals. For example, if this involved a volatile asset, major news or macroeconomic trends could lead to significant deviations that skew outcomes outside the projected ranges.
